questions.stem: A student investigates the reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid by timing how long it takes for a cross drawn under the flask to disappear. What is being measured?

options.text: The volume of gas produced
The time for sulfur precipitate to make the solution opaque enough to hide the cross
The temperature change of the reaction
The change in mass of the solution

questions.explanation: This classic 'disappearing cross' experiment measures the time taken for enough sulfur (an insoluble yellow solid) to form as a precipitate to obscure the cross beneath the flask. A shorter time means a faster reaction. This is a practical way to measure rate when one product is an insoluble solid that clouds the solution.

questions.stem: Which method would be most suitable for measuring the rate of a reaction that produces hydrogen gas?

options.text: Timing how long a cross takes to disappear
Measuring colour change with a colorimeter
Collecting the gas in a gas syringe and recording volume at regular intervals
Measuring the temperature change every 10 seconds

questions.explanation: When a gas is produced, collecting it in a gas syringe (or over water) and recording the volume at regular time intervals is the most appropriate and accurate method. This gives data that can be plotted as a volume-time graph. The disappearing cross method is for precipitate formation, and temperature change measures energy, not rate directly.

questions.stem: On a graph of volume of gas produced vs time, how would you determine the rate of reaction at a specific point in time?

options.text: Read the volume at that time from the y-axis
Draw a tangent to the curve at that point and calculate its gradient
Divide the final volume by the total time
Measure the area under the curve up to that point

questions.explanation: The instantaneous rate at a specific time is found by drawing a tangent to the curve at that point and calculating its gradient (change in y / change in x). Dividing final volume by total time gives only the mean rate over the whole reaction. The gradient of a tangent gives the rate at that precise moment.

questions.stem: A student measures the rate of reaction between calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid by placing the flask on a balance. She records the mass every 30 seconds. Why does the mass decrease during this reaction?

options.text: The calcium carbonate dissolves and becomes lighter
Carbon dioxide gas escapes from the flask, reducing the total mass
Water evaporates due to the exothermic reaction
The hydrochloric acid decomposes and loses mass

questions.explanation: CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. The carbon dioxide gas produced escapes into the atmosphere, causing the total mass on the balance to decrease. The rate of mass loss corresponds to the rate of CO2 production. If the flask were sealed, the mass would remain constant (conservation of mass).

questions.stem: Two experiments measure the same reaction. Experiment 1 uses a gas syringe to collect gas. Experiment 2 uses mass loss on a balance. Which gives more accurate rate data for a reaction producing small volumes of gas?

options.text: Mass loss, because balances are always more accurate
Gas syringe, because it directly measures the gas volume produced
Both give identical results
Mass loss, because the gas syringe cannot detect small volumes accurately

questions.explanation: For small volumes of gas, a gas syringe is generally more accurate because it directly measures even small volumes of gas. The mass loss method may struggle with small amounts of gas because the mass change is very small and may be within the uncertainty of the balance (e.g., losing 0.01 g of CO2 is hard to measure precisely).
